name: William Carey
title: William Carey: learning, translating and persevering in India
description: William Carey, the Serampore mission and the shared work of translation and education, documented by Boston University and BMS.

sections.heading: The question that became a journey
paragraphs: In 1792, William Carey published a reflection on the obligation of Christians to use means to proclaim the gospel among the nations. He was a pastor and had worked as a shoemaker. His proposal was part of the movement that gave rise to the Baptist missionary society known today as BMS World Mission.

Carey arrived in Calcutta in 1793. The first years brought financial difficulties and political obstacles. The Boston University biography explains that he worked managing an indigo plantation in Bengal. His missionary life began within a complex colonial context, with household needs and work responsibilities.

sections.heading: Serampore was a shared work
paragraphs: At Serampore, Carey worked alongside Joshua Marshman and William Ward. Bible translation and publishing also required the participation of many Indian co-workers. Christopher Smith’s article highlights that network of work and the growth of activities in education, linguistics, printing and relief.

Serampore College was founded in 1818. Carey’s legacy includes access to the Scriptures in local languages and educational projects, but it should not be described as if a European visitor had worked alone. Recognizing the Indian co-workers makes the account more faithful and shows how service depends on shared knowledge and skills.

reflection: In 1 Corinthians 3:5–9, Paul presents ministers as servants working on the same project. That image is useful for reading the story of Serampore. Translating requires receiving help, learning from others and admitting limits. A well-known name can stand for a work in which many less-remembered people took part.

The church today can learn from that cooperation and from the effort to understand other languages. Mission requires respect for the communities being served and attention to the social context. Enthusiasm for taking the gospel to others needs to be accompanied by humility, preparation and a willingness to share responsibilities and recognition.
review_note: The colonial context is identified and the Indian co-workers are acknowledged. Not all translations are attributed individually to Carey.
source_labels: Christopher Smith. “Carey, William,” in Biographical Dictionary of Christian Missions, ed. Gerald H. Anderson (1998); available at Boston University, History of Missiology.
